title: From benchmarks to deployment: a comprehensive review of agentic AI evaluation
explain_beginner: This review looks at how we test AI agents, which are systems that can plan several steps, use tools, and interact with their surroundings. It examines 15 widely used tests and finds a big gap. Agents can score well on these tests yet still fail in real work. The tests mostly check whether a task was finished, not whether the agent was safe, affordable, easy to maintain, or fits into existing workflows. None of the 15 scored safety or security, and none included cost in their main scoring. The authors conclude that better testing methods, not just stronger models, are needed for reliable use.
explain_business: For leaders, this review warns that strong benchmark scores do not prove an AI agent is ready for business use. The authors studied 15 major agent tests and found they focus on finishing tasks while missing safety, security, cost, maintainability, and workflow fit. None of the 15 scored safety or security, and none included cost in their main scoring. That means current test results can hide operational, financial, and compliance risks. The practical decision is to require broader evaluations before deployment, covering cost, safety, integration, and reliability, rather than relying on benchmark rankings alone.
explain_practitioner: The authors reviewed evaluation methods for agentic systems that plan, use tools, and interact with environments. They analyzed 15 benchmarks, including AgentBench, WebArena, GAIA, ToolBench, and others, comparing their metrics, datasets, and domains, with software development as the main case. The key finding is that evaluation design, not model ability, is the main barrier to dependable deployment. Finishing tasks and simple pass or fail results hide code quality, security flaws, integration difficulty, planning coherence, resource use, and safety issues. None of the 15 benchmarks scored safety or security, none included cost in primary scoring, and 13 used only simple success or failure. They propose frameworks that score entire action sequences.
